blocks.heading: Individual specialisation
blocks.text: Individual specialisation occurs when a person concentrates on a narrower task or occupation. An invented craft workshop may employ a worker mainly to cut leather accurately while another stitches finished pieces. A self-employed repairer can instead specialise in one category of equipment while completing several stages of each repair. The important feature is the narrower focus, not whether the person has an employer. Relevant practice can build expertise and reduce mistakes. A specialist may also become familiar with a particular tool, material or customer problem. These benefits need to be connected to the task. Repeating a task that is poorly understood does not automatically improve it. Training, feedback and suitable equipment affect whether focused experience turns into better performance.

blocks.heading: Skill and adaptability at the individual level
blocks.text: The specialised worker can face risks when demand changes. If an old repair method is replaced, a narrow skill may be less useful in another occupation. Retraining takes time and can require resources the worker does not readily have. Repetitive work may also become less satisfying, which can affect attention or motivation. An employer might use job rotation or broader training to retain some flexibility, although workers then spend less time on each specialised task and the training has a cost. Compare the expected improvement in normal work with the need to cope with changing tasks. In an individual case, identify the person's actual skill and alternative opportunities rather than assuming that specialisation makes every worker either highly paid or unable to change jobs.

blocks.heading: Regional specialisation
blocks.text: Regional specialisation occurs when an area's production is concentrated in particular activities. A region might develop a cluster of vegetable growers because its soils, water access and climate suit that activity. Over time, skilled workers, equipment repairers, packaging suppliers and transport services may develop around the growers. The resulting network can make the region more effective in serving that production activity. This concentration does not mean that everybody in the area has the same job. Some people work in the main activity, others in supporting services and others elsewhere. Identify the area and its productive focus before explaining the consequences. Shared local conditions can help explain why firms locate together, while links between firms can strengthen a concentration that has already begun.

blocks.heading: A local gain can also create local exposure
blocks.text: When several growers operate in one area, a repair service may have enough customers to employ a specialist irrigation technician. That service can reduce downtime for growers and help support the regional cluster. However, a serious water shortage can reduce crops and also reduce demand for packaging, transport and equipment maintenance. The regional effect goes beyond one producer because linked activities depend on the same base. This is different from a single worker finding a task boring. A region can reduce some exposure by developing alternative activities or more resilient production, but diversification uses resources and may reduce some benefits of concentration. Evaluate the relevant risks and alternatives. Do not treat regional concentration as proof that the main activity causes every local income change.

blocks.heading: National specialisation
blocks.text: National specialisation occurs when a country concentrates production in particular goods or services and exchanges with other economies. A country can develop expertise and production networks in activities suited to its resources and capabilities, then use exchange to obtain other products. It need not produce a single product or stop producing for domestic use. A national pattern is an economy-wide description, not a statement that every firm has the same specialism. Possible benefits include accumulated know-how, a larger market for specialised production and opportunities to spread some costs over more output. The gains depend on production conditions and the terms on which exchange takes place. Topic 7.4 examines the trade reasoning more closely; here identify the country's concentration and the resulting dependence on exchange.

blocks.heading: Export concentration and a national decision
blocks.text: An invented country obtaining much of its export revenue from one crop can gain expertise and a reputation in that product. It may also face unstable earnings if overseas demand falls or bad weather reduces the harvest. Lower receipts can affect producers, linked employment and the resources available to buy imports. These are national consequences because the concentration influences a broad pattern of production and exchange. A country considering more specialisation should compare the likely efficiency gain with the strength of demand, the possibility of disruption and the ability to develop alternatives. More products are not automatically better if the new activities use resources poorly. A conditional judgement explains which concentration is worthwhile, how the risks could be managed and what evidence would justify a different production mix. Transport reliability also affects these choices.
